Random Planted Forest

Source: R/rpf.R
rpf.Rd

Fits a random planted forest (Hiabu, Mammen and Meyer, 2020) for regression or classification. The model is a sum of trees that each split on at most max_interaction predictors, so it decomposes into main effects and interaction components; see predict_components().

Usage

rpf(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'formula'
rpf(
  formula,
  data,
  max_interaction = 3,
  n_families = 200,
  n_splits = NULL,
  split_structure = "leaf",
  n_try_split_points = NULL,
  share_candidates = NULL,
  max_candidates = 50,
  split_decay_rate = 0.1,
  delete_leaves = TRUE,
  min_leaf_rows = 1,
  interaction_constraints = NULL,
  loss = NULL,
  exact_step = TRUE,
  prune = NULL,
  max_panels = 10,
  tune = FALSE,
  purify = FALSE,
  nthreads = 1,
  export_forest = FALSE,
  deterministic = FALSE,
  keep_level_order = FALSE,
  oob_path = FALSE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'data.frame'
rpf(
  x,
  y,
  max_interaction = 3,

)

Arguments

x, y

[data.frame | matrix | recipe], [numeric | factor]: Predictors and outcome for the x/y interface. x holds the predictors, or is a recipe (then supply data instead of y). The predictors need unique names that do not contain :, which joins predictor names in component names such as x1:x2. y is the outcome vector: numeric for regression, factor for classification. A numeric outcome must be finite. A factor outcome needs at least two classes; levels that do not occur are dropped with a warning.

...

Only the old names of renamed arguments (ntrees, splits, split_try, t_try), deprecated: they work, with a warning. Any other (e.g. misspelled) argument is an error. See "Renamed arguments" in Details.

formula

[formula]: A formula with the outcome on the left-hand side and the predictors on the right-hand side, e.g. y ~ x1 + x2. Interaction terms such as x1:x2 or x1 * x2 are an error: they would add a predictor named x1:x2, and : is how components are named. The forest finds interactions itself, up to max_interaction, so list the predictors as y ~ x1 + x2. To fit a product as a predictor of its own, write I(x1 * x2), or add it to data as a column with its own name. Transformed terms of one predictor, such as log(x1), are allowed.

data

[data.frame]: Data containing the predictors and the outcome, used with formula or a recipe x.

max_interaction

[integer(1): 3]: Maximum number of predictors a single tree may split on. 1 fits main effects only (an additive model), 2 adds pairwise interactions, 3 (the default) three-way interactions, and so on. 0 uses all predictors and values above the number of predictors are reduced to it.

n_families

[integer(1): 200]: Number of tree families, i.e. the size of the forest. Each family is grown on a bootstrap sample and predictions are averaged. Was ntrees.

n_splits

[integer(1) | NULL: NULL]: Number of split rounds per tree family. The main tuning parameter: more splits fit more complex functions. A round splits the best of its candidates; near saturation, when every candidate's leaf is too small to split, a round can make no split. NULL (the default) chooses it out of bag while the forest grows (with deterministic = TRUE, which has no out-of-bag rows, NULL means 30). See "Choosing n_splits out of bag" in Details. Was splits.

split_structure

[character(1): "leaf"]: How split candidates are formed and sampled; one of "leaf", "leaf_binned", "tree_then_leaf", "tree_then_all_leaves" or "target_tree_then_leaf". See Details. The names of 0.5.0 ("leaves", "hist", "cur_trees_1", "cur_trees_2", "res_trees") still work, with a deprecation warning.

n_try_split_points

[integer(1) | NULL: NULL]: Number of split points (thresholds) tried per split candidate. NULL means 3 for split_structure = "leaf" and 10 for the other structures. Was split_try.

share_candidates

[numeric(1) | NULL: NULL]: Share in (0, 1] of all possible splits drawn as candidates in each round, capped at max_candidates. NULL means 0.1 for split_structure = "leaf" and 0.4 for the other structures. See "Choosing parameters" in Details. Was t_try.

max_candidates

[integer(1): 50]: Maximum number of split candidates per round.

split_decay_rate

[numeric(1): 0.1]: Down-weights possible splits that were sampled as candidates but not chosen. Each such round ages a split by one, choosing it resets its age to zero, and splits are sampled with weight exp(-split_decay_rate * age). 0 samples uniformly.

delete_leaves

[logical(1): TRUE]: Whether to delete a parent leaf when splitting along an existing dimension.

min_leaf_rows

[integer(1): 1]: Minimum number of rows of the bootstrap sample on each side of every split, so in every leaf, for every split_structure (regression and classification). Split points are tried only among those that keep this many rows on each side, and leaves without one are not drawn (see "split_structure" in Details). 1 means no limit.

interaction_constraints

[list | NULL: NULL]: Feature sets that restrict which interactions the forest may form, e.g. list(c("x1", "x2"), c("x3", "x4")). Each set is given by predictor names or by column indices: with x, the columns of x; with a formula, the predictors in the order the formula names them (y ~ .: the order of the columns of data); with a recipe, names only (its steps decide the columns). A tree on the predictors T is grown only if T is a subset of one of the sets, as with xgboost's interaction constraints. The subsets of a set stay allowed, so the forest keeps the main effects it grows a pair from. A predictor in no set is not used. Applies together with max_interaction: set max_interaction = 0 to let the sets alone decide. NULL means no constraint. One use is to refit the forest on the effects a first fit found, e.g. after dropping its small components.

loss

[character(1) | NULL: NULL]: Loss function. NULL uses "L2" for regression, the only supported loss, and "exponential" for classification (with more than two classes the multiclass exponential loss SAMME). Classification also supports "logit" (the multinomial log-likelihood), and "L1" and "L2", which fit class indicators directly and do not yield proper probability estimates. See "Classification losses" in Details.

exact_step

[logical(1): TRUE]: Only used with loss = "logit": whether the two leaves of each split get the exact minimisers of the penalised loss (Newton's method to convergence on the leaf's rows), or one Newton step from the sums the split search scored them by (FALSE, faster). The split search is the same either way. The exponential loss's step is exact by itself, so exact_step does not change "exponential" fits. See "Classification losses" in Details.

prune

[logical(1) | NULL: NULL]: Whether to return the pruned model instead of the forest: the forest is pruned by prune_components() with its defaults on the training rows, and the result is its rpf_pruned model. NULL (the default) means TRUE, and FALSE with deterministic = TRUE, where TRUE is an error (pruning needs out-of-bag rows). FALSE returns the forest. See "Pruning" in Details.

max_panels

[numeric(1): 10]: Used only when pruning: the most heat maps a kept component of three or more predictors may need; such a component is coarsened to at most max_panels heat maps and the model is pruned again (the max_panels of prune_components()). A whole number of at least 1, or Inf for no coarsening.

tune

[logical(1) | character(1) | rpf_tune_control: FALSE]: Whether to tune the greediness (n_try_split_points, share_candidates) and min_leaf_rows out of bag (not with deterministic = TRUE, at least 10 tree families). TRUE runs the full search (tune_control()), "quick" the two-forest preset, and a tune_control() object your own. Every forest of the search has n_splits chosen out of bag and is pruned, so tune implies n_splits = NULL and prune = TRUE, and giving n_try_split_points, share_candidates or min_leaf_rows with it is an error. See "Tuning out of bag" in Details.

purify

[logical(1): FALSE]: Whether to purify the forest after fitting, which predict_components() requires, with the defaults of purify(). For other settings, call purify() after fitting instead. Not used with prune = TRUE: the pruned model stores the components it keeps.

nthreads

[integer(1): 1]: Number of threads for fitting. Also the default for predict() and purify().

export_forest

[logical(1): FALSE]: Whether to store the flattened forest in the returned object as $forest (with prune = TRUE, in the forest: $fit$forest). If FALSE, it is NULL, which saves memory.

deterministic

[logical(1): FALSE]: Whether to fit without randomness: no bootstrap, the first max_candidates possible splits as candidates (share_candidates and split_decay_rate are ignored) and evenly spaced thresholds. The result does not depend on the seed, and all tree families are identical, so use n_families = 1. There are no out-of-bag rows, so n_splits = NULL means 30 and prune = NULL means FALSE. Mainly useful for testing and debugging.

keep_level_order

[logical(1) | character: FALSE]: Which factor predictors keep the order of their levels instead of being ordered by the outcome. FALSE orders every factor by the outcome, TRUE keeps the level order of every factor, and a character vector keeps it for the named factor predictors only. See "Factor predictors" below.

oob_path

[logical(1) | integer: FALSE]: Whether to track the out-of-bag (OOB) error along the splits (not with deterministic = TRUE). TRUE evaluates it at the checkpoints of oob_path_checkpoints() for n_splits, four per doubling; an increasing integer vector in 1..n_splits gives the checkpoints. The fitted forest is the same as without. See Details. With n_splits = NULL the path of the checkpoints grown is stored either way, and only TRUE or FALSE is allowed.

Value

With the defaults, an object of class rpf_pruned (see below). With prune = FALSE, an object of class "rpf" with model object contained in $fit. With oob_path, $oob_path holds the OOB path: a data frame with one row per checkpoint, n_splits, the corrected and the plain OOB root mean squared error (oob_rmse, oob_rmse_raw), and the standard errors of the two mean squared errors (se_mse, se_mse_raw). Its attribute n_rows is the number of training rows with an OOB tree family. For classification with loss = "logit" or "exponential", or more than two classes, the columns are the mean corrected and plain criterion (oob_loss, oob_loss_raw) and their standard errors (se_loss, se_loss_raw), and the attribute criterion names it (see "Classification" in Details). With n_splits = NULL, $params$splits is the chosen number of splits ($params keeps the names of 0.5.0, see "Renamed arguments" in Details), $oob_path the path of the checkpoints grown, and $splits_oob a list with the chosen n_splits, stopped_at (the number of splits where growing stopped) and capped (whether it stopped at the cap while the error was still falling, neither stop rule reached). When pruning (the default), an object of class rpf_pruned (see prune_components()), whose element fit is the forest (not purified), with the elements above: the pruned model's OOB path is $fit$oob_path, and with n_splits = NULL the chosen number of splits $fit$params$splits and the stop $fit$splits_oob. With tune, the rpf_pruned model of the chosen forest, with an element tune: search, the search table (one row per forest grown, in the order grown: step, n_try_split_points, share_candidates, min_leaf_rows, the chosen n_splits, stopped_at, capped, the forest's corrected OOB RMSE oob_rmse_forest (as the pruning scores it: its rule "D" at tau = 0, which keeps every nonzero component; the OOB path's oob_rmse at the chosen n_splits leaves the rows without OOB families of both halves uncorrected and is higher), its pruned model's rule, tau, n_kept and corrected OOB RMSE oob_rmse (the score; for classification both are the square root of the mean corrected criterion), seconds, whether each step chose it (chosen_step1, chosen_step2, chosen_step3; NA if not a candidate of the step) and final); steps, each step's candidates and choice; settings, the chosen n_try_split_points, share_candidates, min_leaf_rows and n_splits; control, the tune_control() used; and seconds.

Details

By default, rpf() returns the pruned model that can be shown, in one call:

  1. it grows 200 tree families of up to three-way interactions, with the number of splits chosen out of bag while they grow (n_splits = NULL);

  2. it prunes the forest's components by prune_components() with its defaults (prune = NULL): the sparse rule, chosen out of bag;

  3. it coarsens every kept component of three or more predictors to at most max_panels = 10 heat maps and prunes again.

The result, of class rpf_pruned, has methods for predict(), predict_components() and print(). prune = FALSE returns the forest (class rpf) instead, and n_splits = <number> fits a fixed number of splits.

Choosing parameters

The defaults were chosen on 44 simulated data sets and California housing (regression) and carried over to classification.

max_interaction sets which effects the model can represent: 1 for an additive model, 2 to add pairwise interactions, 3 (the default) three-way interactions. Order 3 had 15% lower test error than order 2 on the simulated sets and 1.5% lower on California housing. Higher orders gain only where the truth has such interactions, cost much more time (no limit was 11 to 41 times slower on California housing, and worse there), and the pruned model rarely keeps a component of more than three predictors, so it is shown in at most max_panels heat maps anyway. With a higher max_interaction, splits are spread over more possible components.

n_splits sets how closely the model follows the data. By default it is chosen out of bag while the forest grows (see "Choosing n_splits out of bag"), so it need not be tuned.

n_families averages over bootstrap samples to reduce variance, and fitting and prediction time grow linearly with it. Each tree family is itself a complete model, a sum of trees covering all components, rather than a single tree, but averaging more of them still pays off: the test error fell by about 2% per doubling of the families up to 200 on the simulated sets, and the pruned models were sparser (California housing: 34 instead of 47 kept components at 200 instead of 50 families). Hence the default of 200, at the price of time; use fewer for a quick look.

The split search parameters (split_structure, n_try_split_points, share_candidates, max_candidates, split_decay_rate) trade speed for a more thorough, more greedy search. For "leaf", a less greedy search is better: 3 split points per candidate and 10% of the possible splits per round (the default) had 5.7% to 6.8% lower test error than 10 and 40% (the default of the other structures, and of "leaf" before). tune searches this greediness out of bag.

For classification, "exponential" (the default) and "logit" fit on the link scale and are transformed to probabilities; see "Classification losses". "L1" and "L2" fit class indicators directly and their probabilities are truncated to [0, 1].

Classification losses

"exponential" and "logit" fit scores on the link scale: with two classes one score, the log-odds of the second class; with more, "logit" one score per class but the first (whose score is 0) and "exponential" one score per class, summing to 0 (the multiclass exponential loss SAMME of Zhu, Zou, Rosset and Hastie, 2009, whose row weight is exp(-g), g the score of its class). The probabilities are the softmax of the scores.

Every split moves the scores of the rows of each new leaf by one step, which minimises the leaf's penalised loss: the loss of its rows, plus that of one pseudo-row (split evenly over the classes) at the leaf's current mean score. The pseudo-row pulls the step towards no change, so a leaf whose rows all have one class moves towards a finite level (about log(2 n + 1) for n rows and two classes) and is not moved further once it is there, and no clamp of the class shares is needed. A split is scored by its gain over the parent leaf's own step, and each new leaf pays for its pseudo-row, so splitting a leaf of one class gains nothing, nor does repeating a split whose leaves are at their optimum, and such splits are not made. A round in which no candidate gains makes no split. The candidates' gains come from sums over their two sides (the second-order Newton gain for "logit", the exact gain for "exponential"), built as regression builds its sums (along the leaf's sorted rows, so that a split point costs the same whatever the leaf's size; for "tree_then_leaf" one pass over the leaf per split point). "exponential"'s step is exact; with exact_step = TRUE (the default) "logit"'s steps are made exact too, otherwise they are one Newton step.

Factor predictors

Factor predictors, and character predictors, which are converted to factors, are coded as integers 1, 2, ... in an order of their levels, and splits are thresholds on these codes. A split therefore separates the levels below a cut from those above it in that order.

By default, the levels are ordered by the outcome, so that the levels most alike in the outcome are neighbours (Wright and König, 2019):

  • regression: by the mean outcome of each level;

  • binary classification: by the share of the second outcome level;

  • more than two classes: by the first principal component of the class proportions of each level (Coppersmith et al., 1999).

This applies to ordered factors too. With keep_level_order, the chosen factors are instead coded in the order of levels(), as given, ordered or not, so that every split separates neighbouring levels in that order.

The coding is stored in the fit as $factor_levels, the levels of each factor in the order of their codes. predict(), predict_components() and purify() code new data by these levels, by name, so the order of the levels in new_data does not matter.

split_structure

In each round, a share_candidates share of all possible splits (capped at max_candidates) is drawn as candidates with weights exp(-split_decay_rate * age). split_structure defines what a candidate is and how its split points are tried. The names say the candidate, then how the leaf to split is found.

  • "leaf" (was "leaves"): Split candidates are (leaf, split-dimension) pairs. For each sampled candidate, n_try_split_points split points are drawn uniformly without replacement from the distinct values of that predictor among the leaf's rows, leaving out the smallest and, with min_leaf_rows, those that leave fewer rows on either side (all of them if there are fewer), and evaluated to choose the best split.

  • "leaf_binned" (was "hist"): As "leaf", but split points are drawn from boundaries of quantile bins computed once per predictor, which makes evaluating them faster on large data. With min_leaf_rows, only from the boundaries that leave that many rows on each side, and candidates without one are not drawn.

  • "tree_then_leaf" (was "cur_trees_1"): Split candidates are (current-tree, split-dimension) pairs. For each sampled candidate, perform n_try_split_points evaluations. Each evaluation samples a leaf from the set of valid current trees (with probability proportional to its number of available split points) and then uniformly samples a single split point within that leaf. With min_leaf_rows, a leaf's available split points are those that leave that many rows on each side, so a leaf without one is not drawn.

  • "tree_then_all_leaves" (was "cur_trees_2"): Split candidates are (current-tree, split-dimension) pairs. For each sampled candidate, iterate through every valid leaf. Within each leaf, sample n_try_split_points split points uniformly and evaluate them. With min_leaf_rows, only split points that leave that many rows on each side, and leaves without one are skipped.

  • "target_tree_then_leaf" (was "res_trees"): Split candidates are resulting trees. For each sampled candidate, run n_try_split_points evaluations by sampling a (split-dimension, leaf) pair from all valid pairs (with probability proportional to its number of available split points), then uniformly sampling one split point within that pair. With min_leaf_rows, the available split points are those that leave that many rows on each side, as for "tree_then_leaf".

Renamed arguments

Four arguments and the split structures were renamed after version 0.5.0: ntrees is now n_families, splits is n_splits, split_try is n_try_split_points and t_try is share_candidates; the split structures are listed above. The prefix gives the unit: n_ a count, share_ a share in (0, 1], max_ a cap. The old names still work and give the same fit, with a deprecation warning once per session for each old name (as lifecycle's soft deprecation; options(lifecycle_verbosity = "warning") warns every time, "quiet" never); giving an argument under both names is an error. The fitted model's $params keeps the old names (ntrees, splits, split_try, t_try, and the old split_structure values), so code that reads them, and models saved by 0.5.0, keep working.

The draw of candidates for "leaf"

With split_structure = "leaf" (regression and classification), the global option randomPlantedForest.exact_draw chooses how the candidates are drawn. With FALSE (the default), the candidates are drawn from a Fenwick tree over the weights, kept up to date between rounds, which costs a few random numbers per candidate. With TRUE, the exact draw of earlier versions, every possible split gets a random number in every round. Both draw from the same distribution, but with other random numbers, so the same seed gives another (equally good) forest. Ties between equally good candidates may go to different candidates under the two draws, so with many splits, near saturation, their fits differ in distribution, though not in accuracy. With min_leaf_rows, both leave out the same candidates: those whose leaf has no threshold with that many rows on each side. The fast draw is about 2.5 times as fast on large data with many splits. The option is read when the forest is fitted and stored in params$exact_draw; it does not affect the other split structures. To reproduce a regression fit of version 0.5.0, set it and give 0.5.0's defaults, as the example "A regression forest of version 0.5.0" does:

options(randomPlantedForest.exact_draw = TRUE)

Classification fits of 0.5.0 cannot be reproduced: they changed for every split structure and loss (see NEWS: classification uses regression's split structures, the largest value of a predictor can be split off, and three or more classes with the exponential loss use SAMME).

Reproducibility

With the same seed, rpf() gives the same forest on the same platform, also with more threads. Another platform can give another forest for the same seed, because the integer sampling of the C++ standard library (std::uniform_int_distribution) differs between implementations, such as libc++ and libstdc++.

The out-of-bag path

With the same seed, the forest grown with k splits is exactly the first k splits of every tree family of a forest grown with more: nothing in the fit depends on the total number of splits. Each family is grown on a bootstrap sample, so every training row is out of bag for the families that did not draw it (about 37% of them). With oob_path, each family's prediction at its OOB rows is updated split by split while it grows, and copied at each checkpoint. So one fit gives the OOB error of every forest with fewer splits, for example to choose n_splits without cross-validation. This costs 2 * nrow(x) * length(checkpoints) doubles and a little time; the fit itself is unchanged.

The OOB prediction of a row is the mean over its OOB families, and the plain error (oob_rmse_raw) is the root mean squared error of these predictions over the rows with an OOB family. That mean averages fewer families than the forest, so the plain error overstates the forest's error by the families' extra variance, more so with more splits. The corrected error (oob_rmse) subtracts this excess, (1 / m_i - 1 / n_families) * v_i for row i with m_i OOB families, where v_i is the variance across families estimated from the OOB means over the families of even and of odd index, v_i = (g_even - g_odd)^2 / (1 / m_even + 1 / m_odd); this is also the correction of prune_components()' OOB choice. A row whose OOB families are all even or all odd is not corrected here (prune_components() gives it the mean estimate of the other rows): about 2% of the rows at 20 families, 18% at 10 and over half at 4 (none at 50), so with few families the corrected error is biased upwards, and above the corrected error prune_components() gives the same forest (rule "D" at tau = 0). Factor levels are ordered by the outcome of all training rows: by the mean outcome (regression), by the share of the second class (binary classification) or by the first principal component of the class proportions (three or more classes). So a row's own outcome enters the ordering its OOB families split on, and the OOB error is somewhat optimistic with factor predictors, most so with many levels.

Choosing n_splits out of bag

With n_splits = NULL (not deterministic), the number of splits is chosen while the forest grows, by the corrected OOB error of the out-of-bag path. The families grow to checkpoints, four per doubling of the splits (oob_path_checkpoints() up to 25,600), and the forest's corrected error is followed checkpoint by checkpoint. Growing stops once the lowest error is one doubling of the splits back (for example, no new minimum from 100 to 200 splits), or once it is on a plateau: the lowest error improved over the last doubling by at most getOption("randomPlantedForest.adaptive_tolerance", 1) standard errors of that improvement (paired over the training rows: the standard deviation of the rows' differences in corrected error between the two checkpoints, divided by the square root of their number). A tolerance of 0 stops only on the first rule. Growing also stops at 25,600 splits, with a warning if the error was still falling there. The result is the forest at the lowest error (ties go to fewer splits; a corrected error at or below 0, a correction that overshot, is not chosen unless all are): the forest that rpf() with that many n_splits and the same seed returns. On 52 data sets (44 synthetic, 8 splits of California housing) the first rule alone chose the same n_splits as the lowest error along a fixed budget of 3,200 splits on 50 of them, and a later, lower minimum on the other two, while growing 0.72 of the splits. The plateau stop chose the same n_splits as the first rule alone on all 44 synthetic sets, the 4 California sets tried and 24 classification fits (logit and exponential loss), while growing 10% (regression) to 29% (classification) fewer splits; it matters most on long, flat out-of-bag curves.

The families grow one at a time, nthreads together, each to the stop estimated from the families grown before it. A grown family keeps only its OOB predictions at the checkpoints and a record of its splits (40 bytes a split), from which the chosen forest is rebuilt, without a refit. A family that reaches the estimate waits there with its growing state while the waiting families fit in getOption("randomPlantedForest.adaptive_pause_gb", 1) GB, so that it can grow on cheaply if the stop comes later; otherwise it is freed, and grown again from its seed if needed. The option trades memory for time; the fit depends neither on it nor on nthreads. Growing all families together would hold every family's growing state until the stop: about 18 GB of resident memory (RSS) on California housing (16,512 rows) at 200 families and max_interaction = 3, where the fit one family at a time peaks at 3.4 GB of RSS (2.3 GB of physical footprint; the adaptive fit alone, measured when it was added: n_try_split_points = 3, share_candidates = 0.1, the exact draw, 8 threads).

Pruning

By default (prune = NULL, or TRUE), rpf() fits the forest, then prunes its components with prune_components() at that function's defaults, on the training rows: the rule and the threshold are chosen out of bag (by cross-validation below 10 tree families, with a message), the sparse choice select = "1se", and every kept component of three or more predictors is shown in at most max_panels heat maps before the model is pruned again. The result is the pruned model, of class rpf_pruned, with methods for predict(), predict_components() and print(). It is the same, bit for bit, as prune_components(rpf(..., prune = FALSE), data) from the same random number state, for every interface. For other settings of the pruning (rule, tau, select, select_by, folds or seed), fit with prune = FALSE and call prune_components(). Together with n_splits = NULL, one call chooses the number of splits out of bag, prunes and returns the model to show. Pruning needs out-of-bag rows, so with deterministic = TRUE prune = NULL means FALSE and prune = TRUE is an error.

Classification

A classification forest goes through the same steps (the OOB path, n_splits = NULL, prune, max_panels and tune) with its score columns: one for a binary outcome, one per class otherwise (K - 1 for loss = "logit": the first level is the reference). Every out-of-bag choice is scored by the loss's own criterion, corrected for the OOB family count as above:

  • loss = "L1" or "L2": the squared error of the raw scores summed over the columns (the Brier score, before the scores are truncated to probabilities). With two classes this is the regression criterion of the 0/1 outcome, and the choices are the regression ones, bit for bit.

  • loss = "logit" or "exponential": the log-loss of the probabilities that predict(type = "prob") returns. The correction is its second-order form, (1 / m_i - 1 / n_families) * d' H d / (2 * (1 / m_even + 1 / m_odd)) with d = g_even - g_odd and H = diag(p) - p p' over the free score columns (for the squared error H = 2 I, the correction above).

The pruning keeps or drops a component for all classes, sizes it by its variance summed over the score columns centred across the classes, and fits one coefficient per kept component shared by the classes (see prune_components()). The criterion was checked against the test log-loss on simulated data; the defaults were chosen on regression and carried over.

Tuning out of bag

With tune, rpf() searches the greediness of the split search (n_try_split_points and share_candidates, on the ladder of greediness_ladder()) and the minimum leaf size min_leaf_rows, without cross-validation. Every forest of the search is grown with n_splits chosen out of bag and pruned by prune_components() with its defaults (without the display), and forests are compared by the corrected out-of-bag RMSE of their pruned model (for classification by the root of its mean corrected criterion); the lowest wins. A pruned model at 0 (every candidate's correction overshot, see prune_components()) is not chosen unless all are. The search is coordinate-wise (tune_control()): with tune = TRUE the ladder from 10 / 0.4 to 1 / 0.0125 at min_leaf_rows = 1, then min_leaf_rows 1, 5, 20 and 100 at the chosen point, then the point's two ladder neighbours, about 10 forests in all. tune = "quick" grows two forests, 3 / 0.1 and 1 / 0.025 at min_leaf_rows = 1. The chosen forest's pruned model is returned, with the display at max_panels, and the search in its element tune. Every forest is grown from the same random number state, so the result is the model that rpf(n_splits = NULL, prune = TRUE) returns at the chosen settings from that state.

On 48 data sets (fresh seeds; 44 synthetic, 4 of California housing) the full search had 10.8% lower test error than 10 / 0.4 (the default of earlier versions; no family of data sets worse than +0.9%), and 2.8% lower than 5-fold cross-validation over the same settings at 1/24 of its cost; the quick preset had 9.4% lower test error (worst +0.4%). In those studies a forest was scored with the pruning's choice of the time (the lowest out-of-bag error, R's coefficients fitted in sample); the sparse default of prune_components() used here was not compared there. A search costs about as many fits as it grows forests, and their prunings.

References

Hiabu, M., Mammen, E., & Meyer, J. T. (2020). Random Planted Forest: a directly interpretable tree ensemble. doi:10.48550/arXiv.2012.14563

Wright, M. N. & König, I. R. (2019). Splitting on categorical predictors in random forests. PeerJ 7:e6339. doi:10.7717/peerj.6339

Coppersmith, D., Hong, S. J. & Hosking, J. R. (1999). Partitioning nominal attributes in decision trees. Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 3:197–217. doi:10.1023/A:1009869804967

Examples

# The default: splits chosen out of bag, pruned, every component shown
set.seed(1)
model <- rpf(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars)
model
#> ── Random Planted Forest model ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Regression. Prediction = intercept + the sum of 9 components.
#> Intercept: 20.2843
#> 
#> Components (largest first), importance = share of the variance of the prediction on the training rows:
#>  component importance
#>  disp      3.5%      
#>  cyl       3.4%      
#>  wt        3.1%      
#>  hp        2.4%      
#>  carb      2.1%      
#>  am        1.1%      
#>  gear      1.1%      
#>  drat      0.67%     
#>  vs        0.47%     
#> 
#> How it was chosen:
#>   The forest: 200 tree families of 15 splits (chosen out of bag; growing stopped at 25).
#>   From the forest's 175 nonzero components (purified): those with a share of at least 0.3% of the forest's Var(prediction), as they are (rule D).
#>   Rule and threshold chosen by out-of-bag error (1-SE rule; 5 folds, seed 682372961) among 16 candidates.
#>   Left out: 166 components, shares together 0.4% (largest qsec, 0.16%).
predict(model, mtcars[1:3, ])
#> # A tibble: 3 × 1
#>   .pred
#>   <dbl>
#> 1  20.5
#> 2  20.2
#> 3  25.6

# Classification, the same steps
set.seed(1)
model <- rpf(Species ~ ., data = iris, n_families = 50)
predict(model, iris[c(1, 51, 101), ], type = "prob")
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   .pred_setosa .pred_versicolor .pred_virginica
#>          <dbl>            <dbl>           <dbl>
#> 1      0.990            0.00949        0.000659
#> 2      0.00296          0.976          0.0214  
#> 3      0.00151          0.00189        0.997   

# The forest instead of the pruned model, with x and y, pairwise interactions
# and a fixed number of splits
set.seed(1)
rpfit <- rpf(
  x = mtcars[, c("cyl", "wt", "hp")],
  y = mtcars$mpg,
  max_interaction = 2,
  n_splits = 30,
  prune = FALSE
)
rpfit
#> ── Regression Random Planted Forest ────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Predictors: `cyl`, `wt`, and `hp`
#> 200 tree families with 30 splits each on 3 predictors, interactions to degree
#> 2.
#> ℹ Forest is not purified.
#> 
#> ── Tree growing 
#>      split_structure: leaf
#>   n_try_split_points: 3
#>     share_candidates: 0.1
#>       max_candidates: 50
#>     split_decay_rate: 0.1
#>        delete_leaves: TRUE
#> 
#> ℹ Fit using 1 thread, also the default for `predict()` and `purify()`.

# A factor that keeps its level order: splits separate neighbouring levels
cars <- mtcars
cars$gear <- factor(cars$gear, levels = c(3, 4, 5))
rpfit <- rpf(mpg ~ gear + wt, data = cars, keep_level_order = "gear")
rpfit$factor_levels
#> NULL

# The out-of-bag error along the splits, from one fit
set.seed(1)
rpfit <- rpf(
  mpg ~ .,
  data = mtcars,
  n_families = 20,
  n_splits = 100,
  oob_path = TRUE,
  prune = FALSE
)
rpfit$oob_path[which.min(rpfit$oob_path$oob_rmse), ]
#>    n_splits oob_rmse oob_rmse_raw  se_mse se_mse_raw
#> 12       42 2.557867     2.709333 1.91871   1.895507

# \donttest{
# A regression forest of version 0.5.0: its defaults and the exact draw
old <- options(randomPlantedForest.exact_draw = TRUE)
set.seed(1)
rpfit <- rpf(
  mpg ~ cyl + wt,
  data = mtcars,
  max_interaction = 2,
  n_families = 50,
  n_splits = 30,
  n_try_split_points = 10,
  share_candidates = 0.4,
  prune = FALSE
)
options(old)
# }

# \donttest{
# Tuning out of bag: the quick preset, two forests
set.seed(1)
x <- matrix(runif(400 * 4, -1, 1), ncol = 4, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("x", 1:4)))
y <- x[, 1] + 2 * x[, 2] * x[, 3] + rnorm(400, sd = 0.3)
tuned <- rpf(x, y, n_families = 10, tune = "quick")
tuned$tune$search
